title: Shrove Tuesday
hook: confess and use up the rich food before Lent: pancakes

segments.voice: Yesterday, Candlemas: Simeon holding a baby and calling him light. Your line was a light to lighten the gentiles. Who did you bring a little light to? Day one thousand twenty.

Eggs, butter, milk, a bag of flour, a bit of sugar. On one Tuesday a year, in kitchens across Britain, Ireland and plenty of other places, all of it goes into one bowl and comes out as a stack of pancakes. Lemon and sugar for some, syrup for others, a flip in the pan that lands on the floor at least once. In New Orleans the same day is Mardi Gras, French for fat Tuesday, with parades. It looks like a party, and it is. But the old English name for the day isn't about food at all. It's about the other thing people did before Lent began: they went to church and told the truth about themselves. Today's word is shrove.

To shrive is an old English verb. It means to hear someone's confession and declare them forgiven. Shrove is its old past form, and shriven is what you are afterward: confessed, and let go. So Shrove Tuesday is the day you got shriven, cleared out before the long fast of Lent began the next morning with Ash Wednesday. The letter of James puts the practice of telling your faults to someone else plainly, in the King James Bible: "Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed." Notice the direction there. One to another. Not only up to God, but across, to a person. And the reason given isn't shame. It's healing. Churches practice this differently. Catholics and Orthodox Christians have the sacrament of confession with a priest. Anglicans offer it, and some use it. Some Protestant churches confess together, out loud, in a shared prayer, or between friends. Then the pancakes. Lent was traditionally a time of fasting from rich foods, and in some places that meant eggs, butter and milk. A kitchen full of them on Tuesday night would spoil, or tempt. So you used them up. You cooked everything rich in the house and fed everyone you could. Put the two halves together and the day makes sense. Empty the heart, then empty the pantry. Say what's wrong, then sit down and eat with the people who know. Clearing out and celebrating aren't opposites here. The feast comes after the truth is told.

Here's the practice: a small clearing out. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself, gently, what you'd want to set down before a fresh start. Not a long list. One thing. A sharp word you said. A promise you let slide. Just name it to yourself. If you pray, you can tell it to God plainly and ask to be let go of it. If you don't, simply say it once, honestly, in your own head. Then let your mind turn to food: who could you make pancakes with, or share a meal with, this week? Pick a name. The bell holds the time.
Shrove. The old past form of shrive: to hear a confession and set someone free of it. The day before Lent, named for clearing out the heart.
Your line: shriven and fed. Today, own up to one small thing with the person it touched, and then share some food. Day one thousand twenty.

howItsDone: On the Tuesday before Ash Wednesday, families and churches in Britain, Ireland and elsewhere make pancakes, and some parishes hold pancake suppers or races; in other places the same day is kept as Mardi Gras or Carnival.

myth: Shrove Tuesday is named after pancakes
the name comes from shrive: to hear a confession and forgive.
the letter of James tells Christians to confess their faults to one another
"Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed."
the Bible sets out the pancake custom
the custom grew from the Lenten fast from rich foods; the Bible doesn't mention it.

fork.setup: it's the night before the fast. your kitchen is full of eggs, butter and milk you won't be eating for weeks. what do you do?
options: hide them at the back of the cold store.
throw them out so they can't tempt you.
cook them all up and feed everyone you can.
fork.reveal: the custom is to use the rich food up, cooking pancakes and sharing them, so the fast begins with an empty pantry and a full table behind it.

original.note: Greek: confess (to one another), from James 5:16, the verse behind today's teach.

trapdoor: what it means: the day before Lent when people were shriven, confessed and forgiven, and the rich food was used up and shared.
what a scholar hears: shrive, shrove, shriven, an old English verb for hearing confession; James 5:16 sends confession 'one to another', for healing.
